articles.title: Elderly lady found after incredible community effort
articles.excerpt: A woman in her 70s who went missing in Newhey has been found after hundreds of residents joined Greater Manchester Police in an extraordinary community search.
articles.content_html:
An elderly woman who went missing in Newhey has been found following an extraordinary community effort involving hundreds of local residents.

Christine, who is in her 70s, was reported missing earlier in the evening, prompting an urgent response from Greater Manchester Police and a huge mobilisation across Newhey and the surrounding area.

As concern grew, residents left their homes to help officers search on the ground. People walked streets, paths and open spaces, checked nearby areas and shared information rapidly across community groups in an effort to bring Christine home.

The response was remarkable. Hundreds of people are understood to have assisted either directly with searches or by sharing appeals and helping coordinate information alongside GMP.

At around 11pm, local woman Charlotte Rigby found Christine. In a touching detail after hours of worry, Christine was found clutching a bunch of flowers.

News that she had been located was met with enormous relief across the community, bringing a frightening evening to the best possible conclusion.

Tonight demonstrated Newhey and the wider Rochdale borough at its very best. Residents did not simply share a post and hope for good news. They put on their shoes, went outside and actively helped search for someone who needed them.

Credit must also go to Greater Manchester Police and everyone who supported the search, but special recognition is due to the countless members of the public who gave their time and refused to give up.

The borough should be very proud tonight. This was community spirit in its purest form, and the outcome is the great news everyone had been hoping for.

Out of respect for Christine and her family, no further personal or medical details should be shared unless released through official channels.

articles.title: Shabir Ahmed barred from Rochdale under strict licence conditions as government pushes to deport him
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale grooming gang ringleader is excluded from the borough under his licence conditions, is living under 24-hour supervision at an undisclosed location outside the area, and faces active government efforts to deport him.
articles.content_html:
Shabir Ahmed, the ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang jailed in 2012, was released from prison on licence on 2 July after serving 14 years of a 22-year sentence for multiple rape and sexual offences against young girls. Rochdale Daily can confirm, based on conditions set out by the Home Office and Ministry of Justice, that he is not living in Rochdale and is barred from entering the borough.

His licence conditions include an exclusion zone covering Rochdale and Oldham, electronic GPS tagging to monitor his movements, a requirement to live in approved accommodation staffed 24 hours a day, and a ban from his last known address in Oldham. The Ministry of Justice has said he is subject to the toughest supervision possible and would be returned to prison immediately if any condition were breached.

Ahmed, 73, was initially placed in approved premises in Accrington, Lancashire. After that address was shared on social media, prompting protests in the town and calls from the local MP for his removal, he was moved. The government has not confirmed his current location, and Rochdale Daily will not publish unverified claims about his whereabouts. Speculation of that kind has already forced one relocation and puts bystanders at the shared addresses at risk.

The question survivors and residents have pressed hardest is why he remains in the country at all. Ahmed was stripped of his British citizenship after his conviction, and victims had been led to believe he would be deported on release. It has since emerged that a provision of the Immigration Act 1971 prevents the removal of Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the United Kingdom before 1973, as Ahmed did as a teenager in 1967.

The government says it is exploring every option to remove him. Downing Street has confirmed talks with Pakistan, and a Home Office minister told the Commons that “all options are on the table”, saying the government would not give up its efforts given the nature of his crimes. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to amend the 1971 Act so that people convicted of the most serious offences, including child sexual exploitation, can no longer rely on its protections, and ministers have indicated emergency legislation could be considered.

Pakistan, however, has publicly rejected the request. Officials in Islamabad have said responsibility for Ahmed lies with Britain, where he was brought up, and he is reported to have renounced his Pakistani citizenship, which complicates removal further even if the British law changes. The Prime Minister's spokesman has declined to comment on specific proposals while the talks continue.

The pressure on ministers is cross-party. The Conservatives have proposed amending the government's immigration legislation to close the loophole, with their leader urging ministers to adopt the change and the shadow home secretary suggesting visa sanctions or cuts to aid if Pakistan continues to refuse. Greater Manchester's mayor is among those who have called publicly for deportation, and the MP for Hyndburn, where Ahmed was first housed, has demanded he be barred from the North West entirely.

Campaigners including former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver have criticised the handling of the release, saying victims learned of it through social media and continue to live with fear that the authorities have not taken seriously.

Rochdale Daily will update this article as official information is released. Readers should treat any claim about Ahmed's location that does not come from the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, Greater Manchester Police or the courts as unverified.

articles.title: Decision on 450-Home Development in Bamford Expected This Week
articles.excerpt: The planning committee will decide on a proposal for the first phase of a 450-home development on sports pitches in Bamford, with local objections raised over traffic and green belt concerns.
articles.content_html:
A planning committee will meet on August 5 to decide on a proposal for the first phase of a major 450-home development in Bamford. If approved, the scheme would see 45 homes built on land off Greenvale, marking the beginning of a larger project by developers Wain Homes.

The proposed homes would include a mix of two, three, four and five-bedroom properties, with access provided via a new T-junction on Greenvale. To facilitate the development, Chadwick Farm Barn would need to be demolished. Six of the 45 homes would be designated for affordable or social rent, priced at up to 80 per cent of market value.

Concerns have been raised by local residents, with over 300 objections submitted to the council. Issues highlighted include potential traffic congestion, safety of the planned T-junction, insufficient affordable housing, and the development's impact on former green belt land. Planning papers state that the proposed development would deliver a range of high-quality homes for the local community in a sustainable location.

Despite these concerns, planning officers have recommended the scheme for approval. The local sports pitches are expected to be retained and improved as part of the wider development plan, which is part of the Places for Everyone initiative aimed at building thousands of new homes and jobs across nine Greater Manchester districts over the next two decades.

articles.title: Lord-Lieutenant's visit, a surprise inspection passed and a packed cafe: quite a week for Whitworth's Stronger Together
articles.excerpt: The Whitworth carers' group welcomed the King's representative in Lancashire, retained its 5-star hygiene rating in a surprise inspection, and saw its Community Cafe overflow into the main hall — all in one week.
articles.content_html:
A remarkable week for Whitworth carers' group Stronger Together began with a royal representative at the door and ended with a cafe so busy it spilled into the main hall.

On Monday the group welcomed the Lord-Lieutenant of Lancashire, Amanda Parker, and her husband Robert. Mrs Parker is His Majesty The King's personal representative in Lancashire and the first woman to hold the role in the county in almost five hundred years, and her visit is a mark of how far the volunteer-run group has come.

The same day brought a test of a different kind: an unannounced visit from environmental health officers just before lunch service. The inspectors found everything in order and the group retained its food hygiene rating of 5, the top score, which it has held since Rossendale Borough Council first awarded it in December 2024.

By Tuesday the group's Community Cafe was packed, with every table full and half of the main hall pressed into service to seat everyone.

Stronger Together was founded in 2023 by Angela Forster and Kathleen Proctor, both unpaid carers themselves, after they found there was nowhere locally for carers to turn for support. What began as a weekly coffee morning has grown into something much bigger, now based at The Ashcroft on Market Street, where volunteers serve more than 70 fresh, home-cooked meals every week alongside cakes and unlimited drinks, all free of charge with donation pots for those who wish to give.

The group describes itself as a warm, safe space offering advice and emotional and practical support, with activities including prize bingo, crafts and quizzes, and it runs entirely on fundraising, raffles, donations and grants. A crowdfunded project launched last year added gentle exercise sessions with a qualified trainer, healthy eating advice and a singing group open to all ages and abilities.

Recognition has followed. The founders received a Mayor's Special Award at the Whitworth Business and Community Awards in 2023, with the then Mayor of Whitworth describing the pair as truly inspirational to the community. The group went on to win the Not-for-Profit category at the Rossendale Business Awards, and this summer it was shortlisted for Community Group of the Year at the Pride of Rossendale Awards.

Reflecting on the week, the founders thanked the group's volunteers and supporters, saying the group is truly blessed in the people around it.

Anyone who would like to support Stronger Together, volunteer or find out about its sessions can contact the group through its Facebook page.

articles.title: Are Facebook Groups Becoming the Gatekeepers of Local News?
articles.excerpt: Large community Facebook groups now play a major role in determining which local stories residents see, raising questions about moderation, access to information and the influence of digital gatekeepers.
articles.content_html:
Recent posts from independent local news publishers have, at times, remained pending approval or failed to appear in large community Facebook groups. The reasons are not always clear and may range from routine moderation and administrative delays to editorial decisions made by group administrators.

Whatever the explanation, the situation raises a wider question about how much influence large local Facebook groups have over the news and viewpoints residents are exposed to.

Many of these groups have memberships larger than the circulation of traditional local newspapers. For thousands of people, they have become the primary place where local news, events and community discussion are discovered. Decisions about which posts are approved can therefore have a significant impact on what information reaches the public.

Independent journalism exists to report what is happening within a community, regardless of whether those stories are politically convenient or uncomfortable. It should not matter whether a story reflects positively or negatively on any political party, campaign group or public body. The role of journalism is to inform readers, not to tell them what to think.

Equally, moderation is an important part of running any online community. Administrators are entitled to remove unlawful material, spam, abuse, hate speech or defamatory content. However, where lawful reporting is prevented from reaching large community audiences, it is reasonable to ask whether local people are receiving a balanced picture of events.

Too often, debate can become centred on labels rather than evidence. Terms such as 'misinformation', 'divisive' or 'harmful' should only be used where they can be supported by facts. If reporting is inaccurate, it should be corrected. If facts are disputed, they should be challenged with evidence. Robust debate is healthier than silent suppression.

Independent local journalism has become increasingly important as traditional local newsrooms have shrunk. Smaller publishers often report stories that might otherwise receive little attention, giving residents access to a broader range of information and perspectives.

Ultimately, Facebook groups have become powerful gatekeepers of local information. That influence brings responsibility. While moderators are free to manage their communities as they see fit, readers should also recognise that what appears in a Facebook feed is not necessarily the full picture of what is happening across Rochdale borough.

A healthy democracy depends on people having access to a range of lawful reporting and being trusted to reach their own conclusions.

articles.title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
articles.excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
articles.content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

articles.content_html:
Rochdale Hornets Women will host their first-ever Superhero Day fixture against Leigh Miners Rangers on Sunday, 9 August. The match will take place at The Hive, with a kick-off scheduled for 12pm.

The event aims to celebrate the team's achievements and engage the community, encouraging fans to attend dressed as their favourite superheroes.

Former captain Duane Straugheir expressed his excitement for the event, urging supporters to come down to the Crown Oil Arena and make it a memorable day.

Tickets for the match are available for purchase online, and the club hopes to see a strong turnout to support the team during this special occasion.

articles.title: Rochdale Town Hall Shortlisted for Conservation Award
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Town Hall has been shortlisted for the Royal Institution of British Architects' inaugural conservation award, recognising excellence in conservation architecture.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Town Hall has been shortlisted for the Royal Institution of British Architects' (RIBA) first ever conservation award. The award aims to recognise conservation architecture that demonstrates creativity and sensitivity in transforming and securing historic buildings.

The announcement highlights the significance of the Town Hall's architectural heritage and the efforts made to preserve its historical integrity. RIBA's conservation award is intended to celebrate projects that enhance the character of historic sites while ensuring their longevity.

The shortlist reflects a commitment to maintaining the cultural and historical fabric of communities across the UK. The winners will be announced later this year, with the award ceremony set to take place in London.

This recognition may enhance the profile of Rochdale Town Hall, potentially attracting visitors and fostering greater appreciation for the town's architectural history.

articles.title: Heywood Sports Village Hosts Annual White Ribbon Football Tournament
articles.excerpt: Teams from various organisations participated in the annual White Ribbon Football Tournament at Heywood Sports Village, promoting awareness and unity.
articles.content_html:
A football tournament took place yesterday at Heywood Sports Village, featuring teams from across the council and partner organisations. The event was part of the annual White Ribbon initiative, which aims to raise awareness about domestic violence and promote healthy relationships.

More than 50 players participated in the tournament, showcasing their skills on the pitch. Before the matches commenced, all participants made a pledge in support of the White Ribbon campaign, which encourages men to take a stand against violence towards women.

The tournament not only provided an opportunity for friendly competition but also aimed to foster community spirit and collaboration among various local organisations. It served as a platform to highlight the importance of addressing domestic violence issues within the community.

The event was well-received, with participants and supporters alike expressing their commitment to the cause. Such initiatives are crucial in promoting awareness and encouraging positive change in society.
